name: Anthropic: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections
version: Unversioned live Claude Platform documentation retrieved 2026-10-26

[COI: Anthropic] Recommends JSON encoding untrusted strings, least privilege, sandboxing, screening tool outputs, red-teaming, and continuing output monitoring.

version: Unversioned live documentation and eligibility table retrieved 2026-10-26
evidence: [COI: Anthropic] Zero data retention is enabled per organization and applies to eligible endpoints, models, and features; it does not automatically extend to another organization or third-party integrations.
[COI: Anthropic] Retained data is not used for training without express permission; not using data for training is a different commitment from not retaining it.
[COI: Anthropic] The current HIPAA-readiness path requires a signed BAA and a HIPAA-enabled organization with eligible API features. The page says this arrangement does not also require ZDR.
[COI: Anthropic] The signed BAA is the source of truth for feature coverage; consumer products, Console processing, and external integrations are not included in API HIPAA readiness.
[COI: Anthropic] The feature table marks Files API, message batches, managed agents, code execution, and the server-side MCP connector as ineligible for both listed arrangements at retrieval.

[COI: Anthropic] Under ZDR the API does not automatically block ineligible features; using them steps outside that arrangement for that data. Some client-side tools can be accepted by HIPAA-enabled API requests while remaining outside HIPAA readiness.
[COI: Anthropic] PHI must not appear in JSON schema definitions, including property names, enum/const values, and patterns, because schema grammars are cached separately from message content.
[COI: Anthropic] Processor and compliance responsibilities vary by deployment route; Anthropic-managed APIs must not be conflated with cloud-provider-managed Bedrock or Google-managed offerings.
verification: Full primary-source page retrieved directly, including the feature table. Long response saved by tool.

The vendor page loosely describes PHI as individually identifiable health information. HHS supplies the controlling covered-entity/business-associate context; not every health-related datum is necessarily HIPAA PHI.
HIPAA readiness, ZDR, successful API acceptance, no-training commitments, and end-to-end legal compliance are different properties.

name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0: Core
version: AI RMF 1.0 (2023), official HTML excerpt; page says revision is in progress
evidence: The four functions are GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE; governance is cross-cutting. They are not a checklist or necessarily sequential steps, and risk management continues throughout the lifecycle.

GOVERN 2.1 documents roles, responsibilities, and communication lines; GOVERN 2.3 assigns executive responsibility for AI risk decisions; GOVERN 3.2 differentiates human-AI oversight responsibilities.
GOVERN 5.1 and 5.2 require processes for collecting, considering, prioritizing, and incorporating adjudicated external feedback.

MAP 1.1 documents intended use, users, context, assumptions, limitations, and metrics; MAP 1.4 documents business value; MAP 1.5 documents risk tolerances; MAP 1.6 elicits requirements from relevant actors.
MAP 3.1 through 3.5 address benefits, monetary and non-monetary error costs, application scope, operator proficiency, and human oversight.

MEASURE 1.1 documents risks that cannot be measured; MEASURE 1.3 supports assessors independent of frontline development; MEASURE 2.3 evaluates conditions similar to deployment; MEASURE 2.11 evaluates and documents fairness and bias.
MEASURE 3.3 establishes user and impacted-community mechanisms to report problems and appeal outcomes; MANAGE 1.4 documents residual risks for downstream users.

MANAGE 2.1 considers viable non-AI alternatives; MANAGE 2.4 assigns responsibility to supersede, disengage, or deactivate inappropriate systems; MANAGE 4.1 covers monitoring, appeal/override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.
Both the framework and companion playbook are voluntary.
verification: Full official framework excerpt fetched directly.
caveats: Primary normative framework evidence, not a claim of demonstrated control effectiveness or certification.
Individual category wording has one authoritative source; low independent corroboration should not be mistaken for doubt that the document says it.
These are official NIST identifiers, unrelated to the project's ordinal exam-objective labels.

name: NIST AI RMF Playbook: Govern
version: Living AI RMF 1.0 playbook retrieved 2026-10-26; notice says update follows framework revision
evidence: GOVERN 1.1 explains that legal requirements differ by application and context, and that disparate-impact analysis and demographic-based debiasing can raise different legal considerations.

GOVERN 1.4 suggests documentation covering business justification, scope, assumptions, limitations, alternatives, testing, upstream/downstream dependencies, deployment, monitoring, change management, and stakeholder engagement.
GOVERN 1.5 suggests monitoring and incident-response ownership, mechanisms for impacted people to provide feedback, recourse to contest outcomes, and opt-out mechanisms.
GOVERN 1.7 warns that indiscriminate deletion during decommissioning can increase risk, including regulatory retention, dependencies, and future investigations.
GOVERN 2.1 suggests separating development management from testing, managing conflicts of interest, and defining oversight responsibilities and delegated authorities.
GOVERN 2.3 pairs delegated risk-management authority with resources and executive responsibility.

name: NIST AI 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
version: Final July 2024, NIST AI 600-1, DOI 10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1
evidence: Section 2.2 describes confidently presented false content and fabricated logic or citations that can mislead people into trusting incorrect output.
Section 2.4 addresses exposure and inference of sensitive information, including harmful inferences that are inaccurate.
Section 2.6 identifies unequal performance across subgroups, languages, and dialects, along with harms from assuming equal performance across all groups.
Section 2.7 describes automation bias as excessive deference to automated systems and explains that it can exacerbate confabulation and harmful bias.
Section 2.9 distinguishes direct and indirect prompt injection; Section 2.12 highlights third-party component and data risks, difficult attribution, and even erroneous benchmark labels.
Section 3 states that not every suggested action is relevant to every AI actor; applicability differs for developers and deployers.
GV-1.3-002 establishes minimum performance or assurance thresholds for deployment approval; GV-1.3-007 plans for halting deployment that poses unacceptable risk.

GV-1.5-002 calls for after-action review of incident response and disclosure; GV-1.5-003 retains evaluation and provenance history; GV-1.6-003 includes underlying model versions, access modes, known issues, and oversight roles in inventories.
GV-3.2-001 supports independent evaluations proportional to risk; GV-3.2-004 defines user feedback and recourse mechanisms.
verification: Web fetch could not render PDF; downloaded final PDF directly with HTTP 200 and extracted full text using pdftotext. Capture: /tmp/opencode/ccarp-gov-nist-genai.txt.
caveats: Use the final profile, not the withdrawn April 2024 initial public draft.
A voluntary companion profile, not a replacement for legal requirements or a certification.
Citations and apparent reasoning can themselves be wrong. The profile supplies no universally calibrated meaning for model self-reported confidence.

name: EUR-Lex: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, General Data Protection Regulation
version: Original Official Journal text, Regulation of 27 April 2016, OJ L 119, 4 May 2016; not a representation of all subsequent case law or local rules
evidence: Article 5 requires purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and controller accountability; Article 6 specifies lawful bases rather than requiring consent in every case.
Recital 26 distinguishes truly anonymous information from pseudonymized personal data that can be attributed to a person with additional information.
Article 9 has additional conditions for special categories of personal data; Article 25 requires data protection by design and default; Article 28 governs processor contracts and obligations.

Article 22(1) concerns decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects, not every automated suggestion. Article 22(2) contains exceptions, and Article 22(3) requires safeguards including human intervention, expression of the person's view, and contesting the decision for the specified exceptions.
Article 32 requires risk-appropriate technical and organizational security measures, including resilience, restoration, and evaluation of safeguards.
Article 35 requires a prior data protection impact assessment for processing likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms, including specified high-risk situations.
Article 17 includes grounds and exceptions for erasure; Chapter V, Articles 44-49, governs international transfers rather than imposing a universal EU-only hosting rule.
verification: Direct EUR-Lex requests returned empty HTTP 202 responses. Full EUR-Lex source text retrieved through https://r.jina.ai/https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32016R0679, identifying the original URL as URL Source.
caveats: Primary legislative content obtained via a third-party text proxy, not direct full-text retrieval or independent corroboration. Provenance caveat applies.
Legal applicability depends on facts, jurisdiction, current law, and counsel. No legal advice or exhaustive compliance assessment is provided.
An EU region, a processor agreement, encryption, or a human-review checkbox alone does not establish compliance.

name: HHS OCR: Guidance on HIPAA & Cloud Computing
version: HHS guidance published October 6, 2016; full rendered text retrieved 2026-10-26
evidence: The introduction defines PHI in the covered-entity/business-associate context and says a cloud service provider creating, receiving, maintaining, or transmitting ePHI on behalf of such an entity is a business associate, even when it lacks a decryption key.
Question 1 permits cloud use with a HIPAA-compliant BAA and otherwise complying with HIPAA; covered entities and business associates must conduct their own risk analyses and risk management.
Question 1 explains SLAs can address availability, recovery, return of data, security responsibilities, and use/retention/disclosure restrictions, and must remain consistent with the BAA and HIPAA.
Question 2 states that encryption alone does not satisfy integrity, availability, administrative safeguards, and other applicable requirements.
Question 4 states that OCR does not endorse, certify, or recommend particular technologies or products.

Question 8 says HIPAA generally does not require a business associate to keep ePHI after services end; feasible return/destruction and continued protections when infeasible are addressed through the BAA.

Question 9 allows overseas processing if applicable requirements are met while requiring location-specific risk analysis; Question 10 distinguishes HIPAA requirements from additional contractual audit assurances.
Question 11 excludes information de-identified in accordance with HIPAA processes from PHI treatment; it does not say that arbitrary removal of names constitutes de-identification.
verification: Direct web and HTTP fetches returned 403. Full source text retrieved through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html, identifying the HHS source URL and publication timestamp.
caveats: Primary agency guidance obtained via a third-party text proxy; no independent validation of current legal applicability.
A signed BAA is necessary where applicable but not sufficient for end-to-end compliance. Neither encryption nor ZDR grants HIPAA compliance.
Do not confuse retention of required compliance documentation with a blanket requirement to retain all patient payloads for the same period.

name: FedRAMP: Using a FedRAMP Certified Cloud Service
section: Using a FedRAMP Certified Cloud Service
version: 2026 consolidated guidance in optional early-adoption period; read with gov-fedramp-timeline
evidence: FedRAMP certification is reusable evidence about a cloud service offering; the agency authorizing official still accepts risk for the agency's specific system use, configuration, integrations, and customer-operated controls.
Agencies should confirm use of the certified service version and review the package, inherited controls, provider responsibilities, secure configuration guidance, and ongoing information.
The agency authorization documents what it implements, configures, operates, or inherits, rather than copying the provider's package as though it were the agency system.
Agencies configure identity, logging, monitoring, privacy, incident response, and other applicable controls; complete their own authorization before use; and monitor the service over time.

name: OWASP Transaction Authorization Cheat Sheet
version: Rolling OWASP Cheat Sheet Series retrieved 2026-10-27
evidence: Section 1.1 binds user authorization to significant transaction data; Section 2.6 invalidates authorization or restarts approval when those data change.
Sections 2.1, 2.5 and 2.8 place enforcement server-side, preserve allowed state ordering, and require a final authorization gate tied to execution.
Section 1.5 requires accepting an authorization credential once, with an atomic unused-to-used transition in state shared by accepting servers; Section 2.10 requires per-operation uniqueness.
verification: Full primary OWASP page fetched directly and relevant numbered sections read on 2026-10-27.
caveats: Security design guidance, not proof that an application enforces it or a native Claude authorization feature.
Application inference: bind the reviewed payload and current authority to a durable execution claim, retain unresolved state, and do not infer safe replay from an audit log alone.

name: Amazon Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
section: Retrying and side effects; Reducing client complexity; Same client request ID, different intent
version: Malcolm Featonby, primary practitioner article retrieved 2026-10-27
evidence: [COI: AWS] A timeout can leave the caller unsure whether an operation committed; blindly retrying a non-idempotent operation can duplicate resources or other side effects.

[COI: AWS] The described idempotency contract records a caller-provided request identity and parameters, rejects changed intent under the same identity, and requires atomic durable recording with mutation.
[COI: AWS] Retention and late-arrival treatment are service-specific; some APIs supply this contract, not every API or SDK retry.
verification: Full primary Amazon Builders' Library page fetched directly and relevant sections read on 2026-10-27.
caveats: Vendor practitioner account, not a universal exactly-once guarantee or documentation of Claude tool effects.
Application inference: when the scenario supplies no idempotency or reliable lookup, hold uncertain sends for reconciliation rather than assuming a fresh approval makes replay safe.
